title: Losing yourself in the task
text: Watch a climber on a hard route, a surgeon in the middle of an operation, a pianist sight-reading something difficult but possible, and you may {{1}} a look of absorbed calm. Psychologists call it flow — the state of losing yourself in an activity that {{2}} your skills exactly. The conditions are precise. The task must have clear goals and instant feedback; it must be hard enough to {{3}} boredom at bay and easy enough to prevent anxiety. In between lies a narrow channel where attention {{4}} itself: self-consciousness disappears, time distorts, and the activity becomes its own {{5}}, done not for money or praise but for the sheer doing of it. Flow research began with artists who painted for the sake of it and climbers who took {{6}} that no audience would ever see; the concept has since spread to schools, offices and sport. It carries a lesson for anyone who designs work: people are most satisfied not when tasks are easy but when they are {{7}} matched to ability, with goals that are legible and feedback that is honest. The state cannot be commanded — only {{8}} — and the right conditions work the way dry wood and a struck match do.

gaps.explanation: 'you may notice a look of absorbed calm' — become aware of it; mention would require an audience, and nominate and nag do not fit.
'an activity that engages your skills exactly' — draws them fully into use; entangle = twist together, envisage = imagine.
'hard enough to hold boredom at bay' — keep it away; 'hold at bay' is the fixed idiom, from the image of a hunted animal.
'attention sustains itself' — keeps itself going without effort; suspend = pause or hang, surpass = exceed.
'the activity becomes its own reward' — its own payment; resort and recourse = a source of help in difficulty.
'climbers who took risks that no audience would ever see' — deliberate dangers; rim = an edge, rig = a piece of apparatus.
'when tasks are closely matched to ability' — with a tight fit; covertly = secretly, coarsely = roughly.
'cannot be commanded, only invited' — asked to appear; indict = formally accuse, intern = imprison.
